chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-'Ala' ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'So write for them if you know within them any good and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'You reduce for him from the installments (stipulated amounts) that you had not intended to reduce from them, and you do not increase beyond what is in your mind (your estimation of his ability to pay).'
I asked: 'How much?' He said: 'Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) reduced for his slave one thousand from six thousand.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.فِي نَفْسِكَ: In your mind/intention, referring to the master's internal estimation or agreement
key_terms.مُكَاتَبَة: Contract of manumission where a slave pays a fixed sum for freedom
key_terms.نُجُوم: Stipulated installments or scheduled payments in a debt contract

ai.seo_question: How should a master reduce the debt of a slave under the contract of mukatabah according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the mechanics of *mukatabah* by distinguishing between reducing the number of installments (*nujum*) and altering the total debt principal, a nuance critical for fair manumission contracts. It cites Imam al-Sadiq’s guidance that masters should reduce the scheduled payments without increasing the total sum beyond their initial intent, illustrated by Imam al-Baqir’s precedent of forgiving one thousand dirhams from a six-thousand debt. This reflects the Shia emphasis on benevolence (*ihsan*) in fulfilling Quranic obligations toward slaves seeking freedom.
